newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb generals meet amid power struggle.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb generals meet amid power struggle.

text.p: Bosnian Serb army generals and political leaders met on Friday to try to resolve a tense standoff after the general staff and its commander General Ratko Mladic resisted dismissal orders.

Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who ordered the sacking of the general staff last week, travelled to the northeast town of Han Pijesak to hold talks with the Serb military leadership on Friday evening, army sources said.
Earlier, Serb generals conferred among themselves and issued a statement saying they were "examining the possibility of finding a reasonable solution with the Bosnian Serb republic leadership".
Serb army commanders who served during Bosnia's 3-1/2 war have so far refused to recognise Plavsic's newly-appointed commanders.
Senior army officers dismissed the replacements named by Plavsic as party hacks who lack military schooling.
"Unfortunately, a small campaign is being held against the (Bosnian) Serb republic army with completely unpredictable consequences," General Milan Gvero, one of Mladic's deputies, told Reuters.
He added: "We want this army to be led by well-educated, modern, competent, experienced officers and people who proved themselves and not those whose only quality is obedience to a party."
Although there is deep disagreement about the army's "reorganisation", both political and military officials agree that it is time for Mladic -- a folk hero among ordinary Serbs -- to retire.
The Serb commander, indicted twice by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, is required to quit power under terms of the Dayton peace agreement.
NATO, the United States and western Europe have backed Plavsic in her efforts to dimiss Mladic.

Colonel Vinko Pandurevic, who was appointed as a deputy in the new general staff, said in an interview the changes carried out by civilian leaders were necessary but said Mladic was a "personality beyond reproach".
Pandurevic hinted that Serb authorities would prevent any attempts to extradite Mladic to face war crimes charges before the U.N. tribunal in the Hague.

"General Ratko Mladic will remain in the territory of the (Bosnian) Serb republic and you may be sure that ... all institutions and the people will stand behind this man and that nothing can happen to him," Pandurevic said.
Bosnian Serb political leaders tried and failed to sack Mladic and his general staff last year but the army has been weakened since a peace treaty was agreed in November 1995.
There has been no official reaction to the purge from the Bosnian Serbs' patrons in neighbouring Serbia.
Diplomats say the dismissals suit the interests of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic who is wiping his slate clean of wartime associates to polish up his new peace-making image.
